questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the barrier that lets incumbent parties keep new entrants out.
questions.stem: Your design brief for a transport regulator specifies that two incumbent operators hold route licences and that no third licence will be issued before 2030. Which barrier to entry does this design create?

options.text: A legal barrier, because the regulator decides by decree how many firms may hold licences.
A scale barrier, because incumbents already own the depots and the maintenance sheds.
options.misconception: confuses a legal restriction with a cost-based entry barrier

options.text: A social barrier, because incumbent drivers would refuse to share a road with a newcomer.
options.misconception: assumes informal social exclusion rather than formal rules

options.text: A skills barrier, because a new firm could not recruit qualified engineers for months.
options.misconception: assumes labour scarcity instead of licensed entry control

questions.explanation: A single regulator that rations licences sets the number of firms by decree. That is a legal barrier: scale or skills advantages would still let a newcomer compete if it won a licence.
questions.hint: Ask what the newcomer needs, not what it could save.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Judge whether a single-issue party can be treated as a durable competitor.

stimulus.body: A party has campaigned for two years on a single issue: replacing the district's old filtration plant with a modern one. It now holds nine seats, has no other policy platform, and attracts voters who say they will vote for the plant but not for the party's other positions. The party leader asks the design team whether this can become a durable governing party.

questions.stem: Given that briefing note, which judgement best describes the party's position in the party system?

options.text: The party is a cartel because its positions are dictated by a closed council of long-standing members.
options.misconception: assumes cartel membership follows from any disciplined caucus

options.text: The party is a single-issue vehicle whose support is issue-specific and fragile in general elections.
The party is a green party with a full environmental platform spanning pollution, transport and land use.
options.misconception: mistakes one environmental issue for a full green programme

options.text: The party is a catch-all party that voters assess mainly on economic performance at elections.
options.misconception: treats a narrow issue mandate as though it were broad

questions.explanation: A party supported on one policy need not win support on other questions, so it is a single-issue vehicle. The note names no closed council and no wide programme, so the cartel and green labels do not fit.
questions.hint: Check what members say they would vote for.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the party structure that lets insiders control the top office.
questions.stem: Briefing your client on how a party's national executive is chosen, you note that the rules leave the choice to a committee of long-serving members. Which feature does this describe?

options.text: The party is run by a cartel of insiders who control both membership and nominations.
options.misconception: treats any internal committee as a cartel of insiders

options.text: The party allows any member to stand for the leadership under a free nomination rule.
options.misconception: assumes a closed selection implies an open nomination

options.text: The party is a cartel system in which insiders determine who can hold its highest office.
The party uses a primary in which every registered member chooses the candidate directly.
options.misconception: confuses committee selection with a mass primary vote

questions.explanation: A closed committee choosing the leader lets insiders control access to the top job. That is the defining feature of a cartel party; a primary would let members vote directly for candidates.
questions.hint: Notice who can reach the leadership post at all.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a legislature splits its work between a full chamber and a smaller body.
questions.stem: A legislature you are advising has a full chamber of 300 members and a smaller body of 75 that handles detailed drafting and scrutiny. Explain what dividing the legislature this way does to the policy process.

answer.exemplar: Dividing the legislature creates two linked stages. The smaller body scrutinises and amends proposals in detail, so most technical choices are settled before the full chamber debates them. The full chamber then debates fewer, more general questions and provides the final vote, which concentrates attention and makes the government more answerable for the outcome.

questions.explanation: A smaller body lets detailed drafting and scrutiny happen away from the full floor. The full chamber then concentrates on general questions, which sharpens debate and clarifies responsibility.
questions.hint: Think about which chamber does the detailed work.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Classify a primary rule set by its electorate and nomination thresholds.

stimulus.body: Party rules adopted in 2019: 'Any member of the party in good standing may be placed on the ballot for the internal election of the party leadership, provided the nomination is supported by 100 members. The ballot is then sent to all members, who mark one preference. No new member may join the party in the 60 days before the vote.'

questions.stem: Reading the party rules quoted in the extract, which description of the internal selection is accurate?

options.text: The primary is closed, because only members who joined before the cut-off may vote.
options.misconception: reads a joining deadline as the definition of a closed primary

options.text: The primary is open, because any supporter in the district may request a ballot paper.
options.misconception: assumes an open primary lets outsiders vote

options.text: The primary is closed, because a support threshold of 100 members restricts who may stand.
options.misconception: confuses a nomination threshold with a closed electorate

options.text: The primary is closed to party members but open to any member who meets the nomination threshold.

questions.explanation: The extract restricts voting to party members, so the primary is closed to outsiders. The nomination threshold limits who may stand without widening the electorate, so it is closed among members only.
questions.hint: Separate who may vote from who may stand.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Recognise a plurality outcome and distinguish it from majority rule.
questions.stem: A party wins a district with 34 percent of the vote while its nearest rival has 31 percent. Which electoral rule does this outcome illustrate?

options.text: Plurality rule, because the seat goes to whoever polls the most votes even without a majority.
Majority rule, because the party has defeated every rival taken together.
options.misconception: treats a plurality as though it were a majority

options.text: Proportional representation, because votes are converted into seats through a party list.
options.misconception: assumes a single-member seat is allocated proportionally

options.text: A majoritarian bonus, because the largest party is entitled to extra seats after the count.
options.misconception: confuses a plurality winner with a seat bonus system

questions.explanation: The seat went to the highest vote share without a majority, which is exactly how plurality works. Majority rule needs more than half the votes, and neither proportional allocation nor a seat bonus fits here.
questions.hint: Look at whether the winner has half the vote.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Majoritarian bonus against a broad claim
questions.learningObjective: Assess a claim that a majoritarian bonus promotes broad representation.
questions.stem: A colleague argues that giving the largest party a bonus of extra seats rewards the party that most voters want, and therefore produces a more representative legislature. Evaluate that claim for a design brief on electoral reform.

answer.exemplar: The claim confuses majority support for one option with a mandate for a whole programme. A bonus converts a plurality of votes into extra seats, so a party that won more votes in one round gains representation it did not win from a geographically spread second preference. Because large parties already win seats from concentrated support, the bonus amplifies their share rather than correcting malapportionment. Proportional allocation addresses that problem far better.

questions.explanation: A bonus scales a plurality rather than fixing how seats are distributed across the country. Winning more votes in one round is not a mandate for a whole programme, and proportional allocation targets the distortion.
questions.hint: Separate a vote plurality from a programme mandate.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a second ballot rewards candidates who hold second preferences.
questions.stem: In a presidential race with no outright winner on the first ballot, the second ballot pits the top two candidates against each other. What strategic effect does this arrangement have?

options.text: It removes the incentive to build a broad coalition, because only the first-round leader can advance.
options.misconception: believes a top-two runoff rewards single-candidate appeals

options.text: It rewards candidates who can attract second preferences, because first-round votes often split.
It guarantees a majority government, because the winning candidate must then hold a majority.
options.misconception: assumes a runoff always produces an absolute majority

options.text: It favours third parties, since voters can pool their first-round votes behind a minor candidate.
options.misconception: thinks minor candidates gain seats rather than votes

questions.explanation: A runoff concentrates the second preferences of eliminated candidates, so candidates who can hold those voters gain support. A majority is not guaranteed, since the runoff winner may still fall short of half the votes.
questions.hint: Think about voters who back the eliminated candidate.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a consent veto from other barriers to entry.

stimulus.body: A design review notes that in one region two parties have not contested a by-election in eleven years, share a single newspaper, and rotate the position of local registrar between them. New parties that try to register must obtain the consent of the two established party secretaries first.

questions.stem: Given the review note, which barrier to entry does the registration consent requirement create?

options.text: A scale barrier, because the established parties can spread fixed costs over many districts.
options.misconception: confuses shared facilities with a legal veto on entry

options.text: A ballot-access barrier, because the established parties control the printing of ballots.
options.misconception: assumes ballot printing rights rather than consent rights

options.text: A legal barrier, because a veto held by incumbents blocks entry regardless of a newcomer's merits.
A party-financing barrier, because donations cannot be raised without a prior membership.
options.misconception: reads a consent veto as a funding restriction

questions.explanation: Incumbents' consent is a legal veto, so a competent newcomer can still be kept off the ballot. Shared facilities or printing rights would add cost or friction, but would not bar a party from registering.
questions.hint: Ask what a capable newcomer still cannot do.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why single-issue parties usually fail to become durable competitors.
questions.stem: A party in your survey region has campaigned only on hospital funding for four elections and never adopted a wider platform. Explain why this pattern usually prevents it from becoming a durable competitor in the party system.

answer.exemplar: Support for a party built on one policy is conditional on that policy being live. Once the hospital funding decision has been made, the party has no reason to exist at the next election, because it has never told voters what it would do about anything else. Voters who want broader platforms will drift to parties that offer them, and the single-issue party never accumulates the durable identity needed to survive a change of issue.

questions.explanation: Support tied to a single live policy evaporates once that policy is settled. With no wider platform the party never builds a durable identity, so voters defect when the issue changes.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to support once the issue is resolved.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify how a shortlist drawn from past executives restricts access to the leadership.
questions.stem: The committee that shortlists candidates for a party's national leadership is drawn only from members who served on the party's previous executive. What does this arrangement produce?

options.text: An open contest, because every member may still write to the committee asking to be considered.
options.misconception: treats written requests as a route into the shortlist

options.text: A leadership election, because the committee merely screens candidates before a wider vote.
options.misconception: assumes a screening body is followed by a membership ballot

options.text: A cartel of insiders, because only those already inside the organisation can reach the top post.
A merge with any faction that submits a nomination in time.
options.misconception: confuses a nomination window with party merger

questions.explanation: Shortlisting from past executives means only people already inside can reach the leadership. That closes the top job to newcomers regardless of support, which is the cartel feature.
questions.hint: Look at who can realistically reach the top.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a chamber's power to amend gives it over the text of legislation.
questions.stem: In a two-chamber legislature, a bill must clear the larger chamber before the smaller body may consider it, and the smaller body can return amendments that the larger one must then accept or reject. What does this arrangement do?

options.text: It lets a smaller body shape the text of legislation the larger body must then accept or overturn.
It lets the smaller body block all legislation, since it may amend any measure at any stage.
options.misconception: reads amendment power as an absolute veto

options.text: It separates the drafting of laws from the scrutiny of the chamber that passes them.
options.misconception: assumes drafting and scrutiny fall to different chambers

options.text: It removes the need for the larger chamber to debate, because measures there are already settled.
options.misconception: believes a procedural sequence eliminates debate

questions.explanation: The smaller body shapes text that the larger chamber must accept or overturn. That is the point of the arrangement, though it is not an absolute veto since the larger chamber can refuse.
questions.hint: Consider who rewrites the text last.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Classify a primary by the membership rule that defines its electorate.
questions.stem: Under the rules of one party, only members who joined more than ninety days before the primary day may vote, while any member may stand. How should this arrangement be classified?

options.text: An open primary, because the electorate is defined by residence rather than party membership.
options.misconception: confuses a residency rule with an open primary

options.text: A closed primary, because only pre-existing party members may take part in the vote.
A semi-open primary, because a joined member may vote but a non-member may not.
options.misconception: treats a cut-off date as a separate category

options.text: A nomination-only contest, because the ninety-day rule bars anyone from reaching the ballot.
options.misconception: confuses a voting cut-off with a nomination bar

questions.explanation: A closed primary lets only existing members vote, and the ninety-day cut-off simply defines that membership. It limits who votes, not who may stand, and residence plays no part in the rule.
questions.hint: Focus on who casts the ballot, not who files.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how plurality and majority rules differ in allocating a single seat.
questions.stem: A client asks why a candidate can win a seat in your design brief's district with far fewer than half the votes, and what would change under majority rule. Explain the difference between the two allocation rules.

answer.exemplar: Under plurality rule the seat goes to the candidate with the most votes, so a candidate with 34 per cent can win a three-way race in which the leading candidate's rivals split the rest. This maximises the chance of producing a seat and rewards the most popular single option, but it also allows a party to hold a seat that most of the electorate rejected. Under majority rule a candidate must win more than half the votes, so if nobody does the contest goes to a second round in which the leading candidates face each other.

questions.explanation: Plurality awards the seat to the largest single share, so a winner can fall well short of half. Majority rule needs more than half and usually forces a second round rather than settling the seat at once.
questions.hint: Compare the threshold each rule sets.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Majoritarian bonus against a broad claim
questions.learningObjective: Assess what a seat bonus does to the balance of a chamber.

stimulus.body: Electoral review, district by district: after votes are converted to seats in a 60-seat chamber, the party with the largest vote share is given four extra seats. The review notes that the largest party's seats rise from 21 to 25 while the party with the second largest share loses no seat. Support for a full legislative programme remains at 38 per cent of voters.

questions.stem: On the basis of the review, which statement about the majoritarian bonus is correct?

options.text: The bonus raises the number of parties that can win seats, because extra seats spread support.
options.misconception: assumes a bonus disperses rather than concentrates seats

options.text: The bonus is a fair correction, since a party with 38 per cent of voters cannot govern.
options.misconception: treats one vote share as a full programme mandate

options.text: The bonus concentrates advantage, since it adds seats to the leading party without any new votes.
The bonus is neutral, because the leading party would have won those seats under proportional rules.
options.misconception: assumes the bonus reproduces the proportional outcome

questions.explanation: Adding seats to the leading party after conversion raises its total without a single new vote. That concentrates advantage, and the review shows no gain in the number of parties represented.
questions.hint: Ask whose seat total moves and why.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify a second-round trade and the conditions it requires.
questions.stem: A candidate trails badly after the first ballot of a presidential contest and calls on supporters to back the leading candidate instead. What tactical pattern does this represent?

options.text: A plurality strategy, because the candidate hopes to win on first preferences alone.
options.misconception: treats an endorsement as a first-round vote strategy

options.text: A barrier strategy, because the candidate is keeping rivals out of the second round.
options.misconception: confuses a second-round endorsement with exclusion

options.text: A negative campaign, because the candidate attacks the leader to weaken their support.
options.misconception: assumes an endorsement is an attack on the leader

options.text: A second-round trade, because the candidate trades withdrawal for influence or a post.

questions.explanation: Withdrawing in the second round in return for influence is the classic second-round trade. It depends on a second ballot existing and positions being negotiable, which the tally alone does not show.
questions.hint: Notice what the candidate offers in exchange.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Classify a cost-based barrier to entry in a regulated market.
questions.stem: A regulator publishes a fee schedule that recovers only a fifth of its administrative costs, and industry associations say newcomers cannot afford the compliance team the rules require. Which barrier does the note describe?

options.text: A scale barrier, because fixed compliance costs fall hardest on a firm operating at small volume.
A legal barrier, because the regulator has set rules that only incumbents can satisfy.
options.misconception: confuses a cost burden with a rule only incumbents can meet

options.text: A social barrier, because industry associations discourage members from helping newcomers.
options.misconception: reads association membership as exclusion of new firms

options.text: A franchise barrier, because the licence holder owns the only compliant testing facility.
options.misconception: assumes exclusive facilities rather than staffing costs

questions.explanation: Compliance costs that do not scale with output fall hardest on small operators, a scale barrier to entry. A legal barrier would be a rule incumbents alone can meet; this schedule applies to everyone equally.
questions.hint: Check whether the cost depends on firm size.

questions.learningObjective: Judge what survey evidence shows about the basis of a party's support.

stimulus.body: Regional party survey, third wave: 'The party founded to oppose a new landfill site has no stated position on hospital finance, policing, or transport. Membership grew from 400 to 1,900 after the issue appeared in the news.'

questions.stem: Given the survey extract, which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: The party has become a durable competitor, because its membership has grown eightfold.
options.misconception: treats rapid membership growth as lasting electoral strength

options.text: The party remains tied to one issue, since members support the cause rather than a programme.
The party is a cartel, because insiders control who may join and what positions are taken.
options.misconception: infers cartel structure from a single-issue party's identity

options.text: The party is a broad green movement, because its members share a concern for the environment.
options.misconception: confuses a shared concern with a comprehensive programme

questions.explanation: The extract ties membership to one protest and to voting on that issue alone, so the party is issue-based. A membership surge in a news cycle says nothing about durability, and no closed or wide programme appears.

questions.learningObjective: Recognise cartel control of a top office from the rules that fill it.
questions.stem: A party's national leadership is chosen by a closed panel of nine members appointed for life, and no candidate from outside the panel has ever been considered. Which conclusion follows from this arrangement?

options.text: The party must contest every election, because a closed panel cannot organise a campaign.
options.misconception: infers campaign weakness from a closed selection panel

options.text: The party's leader will be confirmed by a wider vote, because no body may select alone.
options.misconception: assumes confirmation is legally required after selection

options.text: The party behaves as a cartel, because insiders control the top office and exclude outsiders.
The party is a single-issue party, because insiders agree on one policy and nothing else.
options.misconception: equates internal closure with a one-issue identity

questions.explanation: A closed, permanent panel that alone chooses the leader means insiders control the top office. No outsider has been considered, which is the cartel pattern, not evidence of a narrow policy.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how an amending chamber shapes the agenda of the larger one.
questions.stem: A legislature's smaller chamber can amend any measure sent to it, and the larger chamber must either accept the amendments or send the bill back. How does this shape the larger chamber's agenda?

options.text: It frees the larger chamber to work on entirely new business, because nothing returns to it.
options.misconception: assumes amendments never return to the full chamber

options.text: It lets the larger chamber set the order of business without consulting the smaller one.
options.misconception: believes agenda control is unaffected by the other chamber

options.text: It lets the larger chamber veto the smaller chamber's membership and composition.
options.misconception: assumes the amending chamber controls the other

options.text: It guarantees the larger chamber a second reading of anything the smaller body changes.

questions.explanation: Because the larger chamber must accept or reject amendments, every change returns for a decision. Its involvement in the measure is therefore guaranteed rather than optional, which shapes the agenda.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Design nomination and voting rules that keep selection open without capture.
questions.stem: Your party wants a leadership contest that any member can enter but that insiders cannot rig. Propose a set of nomination and voting rules, and justify how they balance openness against capture.

answer.exemplar: Separate access to the ballot from the membership of the voting body. Allow any member in good standing to be nominated on a short form requiring a modest number of signatures, so that scrutiny is not a barrier to entry. Publish the nomination threshold and the timetable in advance, and let the membership vote by secret ballot with transferable preferences. Ban officials from helping to gather signatures and require disclosure of who collected them, because the real risk in open primaries is not the ballot but the machinery around it.

questions.explanation: Openness has two parts, who may stand and who may vote, and they need not match. A published threshold and secret ballot let any member enter while making the machinery hard to control.
questions.hint: Split the question into two separate rules.

questions.learningObjective: Apply plurality rule to a reported vote distribution.

stimulus.body: A constituency of 40,000 voters is split between three candidates. Candidate One has 14,000 votes, Candidate Two 13,500 and Candidate Three 12,500. The returning officer notes that Candidate One's share is below the 20,000 votes required for an outright majority, and asks whether the seat is already decided.

questions.stem: What should the returning officer report about the result of this contest?

options.text: A winner is determined, because under plurality rule Candidate One takes the seat with 14,000 votes.
No result is possible, because a seat may never be awarded without an absolute majority.
options.misconception: believes every seat requires an absolute majority

options.text: A second round is required, because the leading candidate has fewer votes than the threshold.
options.misconception: applies a majority threshold to a plurality contest

options.text: The seat is void, because three candidates split the vote below the majority requirement.
options.misconception: treats a split vote as invalidating the election

questions.explanation: Plurality rule awards the seat to the highest vote total, so Candidate One wins with 14,000 votes. No second round is needed, since that belongs to majority rules where a candidate must pass a threshold.
questions.hint: Check the rule the returning officer is applying.

questions.stem: A bill would give the party with the most votes three extra seats after proportional allocation. Which criticism of the proposal is strongest?

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how first-round standings shape second-round bargains between candidates.
questions.stem: In the presidential race described in your brief, the leader holds 38 per cent, the runner-up 34 per cent and the third 28 per cent, and the constitution requires a second ballot if nobody clears 50 per cent. Explain how these figures shape the bargaining that follows.

answer.exemplar: The leader's 38 per cent is short of a majority, so the race is not settled, but the leader is still the only candidate who can probably assemble a majority without renegotiating. That makes the leader's willingness to deal with the runner-up the decisive variable, and the runner-up knows that a split with the third candidate cannot deliver a majority either. The third candidate is therefore in the weakest position and will seek a withdrawal payment or a policy concession, while the leader will try to keep that payment small by persuading the runner-up that the third's voters are not transferable.

questions.explanation: A leader short of the threshold still bargains most strongly; the last-placed candidate bargains least. The second ballot rewards whoever can absorb another candidate's supporters, at a price that gets negotiated.
questions.hint: Consider who needs whom more.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Read coordination evidence in a market regulator's assessment.

stimulus.body: Regulator's competition assessment: 'Two firms hold 71 per cent of the market for regional freight. The regulator has recommended removing the route licensing requirement, which currently guarantees each incumbent a fixed route. The regulator notes that the two firms have already signed a joint rate schedule covering 40 per cent of the network and have never competed on price for a scheduled service in the last nine years.'

questions.stem: According to the extract, what does the joint rate schedule show about the structure of this market?

options.text: It shows that the firms charge low prices, because competition has kept fares down for years.
options.misconception: infers price competition from a shared rate schedule

options.text: It shows that route licensing protects consumers, because it guarantees a service on every route.
options.misconception: assumes guaranteed coverage must mean low fares

options.text: It shows coordination without competition, since a joint schedule replaces price setting by rivals.
It shows that a third firm would face a scale barrier, because the incumbents are larger.
options.misconception: jumps from observed conduct to a cost-based barrier

questions.explanation: A joint rate schedule covering most of the network is price fixing, so the firms coordinate rather than compete. Route licensing is a separate legal barrier, and the extract says nothing about a third firm's costs.
questions.hint: Ask what a shared price list means in practice.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why an internal party leadership contest may not make a party competitive.
questions.stem: Explain, for a design brief on party reform, how choosing a party leader in a closed internal contest can leave the party poorly placed in a general election, even when the contest itself is fiercely fought.

answer.exemplar: An internal contest measures support among people who already belong to the party, so the winner may be a mediocre candidate who is popular with activists and unknown to most voters. The campaign is fought over the preferences of a narrow group, which rewards organisation and ideological signalling rather than media presence or broad appeal. The party then nominates a figure it cannot explain to the electorate, and the general election is effectively a first public appearance. This is the danger of treating internal popularity as evidence of electoral strength.

questions.explanation: A closed contest measures support only among members, rewarding organisation over public appeal. The party may then nominate a candidate it cannot explain to voters, so a strong internal campaign can still lose.
questions.hint: Ask who the contest actually measures.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Majoritarian bonus against a broad claim
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a majoritarian bonus changes seat allocation arithmetic.
questions.stem: A design brief asks you to explain, in plain terms, what a majoritarian bonus does to the arithmetic of seat allocation and why it produces a different chamber from proportional allocation alone.

answer.exemplar: Under proportional allocation every vote is converted in the same way for every party, and the chamber reflects the distribution of votes across the country. A majoritarian bonus breaks that symmetry: after the ordinary conversion, the party with the largest vote share is given extra seats that no vote actually paid for. The result is a chamber in which that party's total exceeds the share of seats its votes would otherwise justify. The bonus therefore works on top of proportionality rather than correcting any error in it, and the size of the gap depends on the size of the bonus.

questions.explanation: Proportional conversion treats every vote alike, while a bonus adds seats to the largest party afterwards. The chamber then over-represents that party relative to its vote share, and the gap grows with the bonus.
questions.hint: Separate the conversion from the bonus.

options.misconception: treats a second place as half a seat

options.text: The candidate will be eliminated, because the constitution allows only one round of voting.
options.misconception: assumes a single ballot excludes second-place candidates

options.text: The candidate is a serious contender, because second preferences can be decisive in the runoff.

questions.explanation: A candidate strong enough to come second everywhere is close to winning and holds a large pool of first preferences. In a runoff that pool of transferable preferences is exactly what decides the final vote.
questions.hint: Think about transferable second preferences.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Design reforms that would open a cartel-dominated party system.
questions.stem: Your design brief notes that one region has had no new party registered for twenty years and that the two established parties divide the districts and rotate the offices between them. Propose reforms that would make entry possible, and justify each one.

answer.exemplar: Start with registration, because consent rules are the cheapest barrier to remove. Require that a new party be registered on application after meeting transparent criteria such as a minimum number of registered members spread across several districts, and remove any requirement to obtain the consent of existing parties. Second, address the shared machinery: give every registered party equal access to ballot facilities and free space, and prohibit arrangements such as the rotation of offices that distribute posts between incumbents. Third, widen participation by making registration easy and low cost. None of these reforms creates a healthy party system on its own, but together they remove the specific points at which entry is currently blocked.

questions.explanation: Cartel barriers work through consent, shared machinery and restricted participation, so each needs its own reform. Registration reform opens the door, while ballot and office rules stop incumbents hoarding competition.
questions.hint: Find each point where entry is blocked.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a cartel maintains barriers to entry without overt collusion.
questions.stem: Explain, for a competition brief, how a settled party cartel can keep new parties out of the electoral market without ever signing a formal agreement to do so.

answer.exemplar: Cartels survive without paperwork because exclusion can be reproduced by separate, defensible-seeming decisions. A regulator that consults the established parties before licensing anyone hears their objections first. A broadcaster that allocates scarce slots by tradition, or by asking who has always appeared on it, closes access without announcing a policy. A party that controls the nomination process can simply decline to support newcomers, and a shared newspaper can treat them as unremarkable. Each step looks like an individual judgement, yet the cumulative effect is a closed market in which entrants never get the access that would let them compete.

questions.explanation: Cartel exclusion needs no contract when each step favours insiders who control the access points. Separate licensing, broadcasting and nomination decisions then reproduce a closed market without collusion.
questions.hint: Look for who controls each access point.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Assess a proposal to appoint party leaders from outside the membership.
questions.stem: A reform proposal would let a party appoint its leader from outside the membership on the argument that outsiders bring fresh ideas and cannot be captured by insiders. Evaluate the proposal for a design brief on party organisation.

answer.exemplar: The proposal confuses two separate problems. Fresh policy input can be obtained without giving outsiders control of the party, through open consultation, a policy commission with external members, or a transparent route for any member to submit proposals. The genuine problem with cartel leadership is that the insiders capture the organisation itself: they set the timetable, decide who can reach the shortlist, and control the resources of the movement. Handing the top job to an outsider does not attack any of that, and it has real costs. The appointee owes no loyalty to the members, has no base to build, and can be replaced by the same insiders at the next review. The reform would change the person at the top while leaving the capture intact.

questions.explanation: The proposal changes the person at the top rather than the capture of the organisation. An appointee with no base and no loyalty to members leaves insider control of the machinery intact.
questions.hint: Ask what stays the same after the change.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the trade-off between open and closed party primaries.
questions.stem: Set out, for a design brief on party reform, why a party that opens its leadership primary to all supporters and a party that closes it to members are making different bets, and what each risks.

answer.exemplar: An open primary treats the leadership as something to be decided by the wider audience rather than the organisation. It lowers the barrier to a challenge, which can renew a party that has stopped attracting recruits, and it makes the choice hard for insiders to manipulate. The risk is that a well-organised external group can capture the contest, and that a candidate chosen for media appeal may not command the activists who actually campaign. A closed primary protects the organisation from that risk and keeps the choice among people with long-standing commitment, but it also lets the incumbent network choose its own successor and signals to outsiders that the party is closed. Neither is safe; the question is which failure the party can better afford.

questions.explanation: An open primary broadens the pool and risks external capture; a closed one protects the organisation from that. The real question is which failure the party can better afford, not which rule is abstractly fairer.
questions.hint: Ask what each rule is protecting.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain what structural change would give a green party a durable footing.
questions.stem: A green party in your survey region has won a seat and then lost it when a single environmental issue was resolved. Explain, drawing on the party's position, what structural change would give it a durable electoral footing.

answer.exemplar: The party's problem is that its vote was conditional on a live issue rather than on a view of the world, so the seat disappeared when the issue did. A durable footing requires an identity that survives the resolution of any particular campaign. In practice that means adopting a broad programme covering several policy areas, so that voters who agree with one position but not another still have a reason to return. It also means internal procedures that keep the programme under revision, because a fixed set of positions ages as fast as a single issue resolves. Building an organisation capable of debating and updating a platform is what distinguishes a durable green party from a pressure group that wins once and disappears.

questions.explanation: A vote won on a live issue vanishes when it resolves, so durability needs an identity broader than one demand. That requires a multi-issue programme and procedures that keep revising it, as in any durable party.
questions.hint: Ask what keeps voters after the issue closes.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the criticism of a leadership contest that its own audit data supports.

stimulus.body: Internal audit of the leadership election: 'Forty-one candidates submitted nomination papers and 38 were placed on the ballot. Of the 19,400 members entitled to vote, 6,850 cast a ballot. Twenty-six of the candidates had served on the party's executive in the previous term, and the winner was the sitting deputy leader, elected with 2,940 votes. The audit recommends that nomination papers be countersigned by a regional officer, and that the executive may co-opt up to six additional candidates in the event of a short ballot.'

questions.stem: Which criticism does the audit data support most strongly?

options.text: The contest was too small to be legitimate, because only 6,850 members voted.
options.misconception: treats low turnout as invalidating the result

options.text: The executive was able to shape the choice, because co-option rights let it influence the ballot.
The nomination stage was too closed, because most candidates came from the executive.
options.misconception: assumes executive members are barred from standing

options.text: The ballot was too wide, because 41 candidates confused voters who abstained.
options.misconception: blames abstention on the number of candidates alone

questions.explanation: The audit concedes the point: a power to co-opt candidates is a power to shape the ballot. With countersignature by a regional officer, the executive sits on both sides of the contest.
questions.hint: Read the recommendation, not just the data.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how chamber balance and chamber function can be designed to work together.
questions.stem: A legislature's smaller chamber is appointed in proportion to the votes in the larger one, and it must approve the larger chamber's bills. What feature of the two-chamber design does this arrangement demonstrate?

options.text: That the smaller chamber is a rival power able to block the larger one outright.
options.misconception: assumes proportional appointment implies a veto

options.text: That the two chambers are elected in identical ways by the same electorate.
options.misconception: confuses proportional appointment with direct election

options.text: That chamber balance and chamber function are designed to work together.
That the smaller chamber duplicates the larger one in every respect.
options.misconception: assumes a drafting body repeats the full chamber

questions.explanation: Proportional appointment makes one chamber reflect the other, and its approval right gives it a defined function. The design ties balance to work: a body mirroring the chamber must also do what the other cannot.
questions.hint: Ask what the arrangement ties together.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Select the primary option that addresses a stated organisational problem.

stimulus.body: Rules review group note: 'Option one keeps the primary to members in good standing at the cut-off date and requires nominations to be countersigned by two branch secretaries. Option two allows any registered supporter who has paid a small fee to vote, on the same ballot, with nominations made by the requisite number of members. The review notes that the fee has kept turnout low and that the same small group has provided signatures in each of the last three contests.'

questions.stem: On the evidence in the note, which option better addresses the concern raised?

options.text: Option one, because the countersignature requirement widens the pool of candidates.
options.misconception: mistakes a restriction for an opening of the contest

options.text: Option two, because a small fee makes participation cheap for ordinary supporters.
options.misconception: ignores the note's finding on low turnout

options.text: Option one, because party membership is a better filter than a payment.
options.misconception: asserts quality without evidence about capture

options.text: Option two, because it removes the secretariat gatekeeping identified in the note.

questions.explanation: The note's complaint is that a small circle signs every nomination, which is gatekeeping in practice. Option two keeps signatures but draws the vote from a broad body of paying supporters.
questions.hint: Identify the specific practice complained of.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Majoritarian bonus against a broad claim
questions.learningObjective: Critique the plurality-based reasoning behind a seat bonus.
questions.stem: A proposal awards additional seats to the party with the largest number of votes, on the stated ground that voters should see a clear winner. Which argument is the strongest objection to that reasoning?

options.text: A large plurality is not a majority, so the extra seats may exaggerate a minority preference.
Clear winners reduce turnout, because voters see their effort has no effect.
options.misconception: assumes turnout falls whenever a result looks clear

options.text: Additional seats require a fresh election, since the original result no longer stands.
options.misconception: invents a re-election requirement for seat adjustments

options.text: Voters already express a majority preference, since the largest share is always above half.
options.misconception: assumes the largest vote share is always a majority

questions.explanation: The justification treats the largest vote share as a popular verdict, but a plurality is not a majority. On that reasoning the extra seats can hand a party a position most voters did not support.
questions.hint: Compare plurality with majority directly.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why transferable second preferences change first-round strategy.
questions.stem: Working through a two-round presidential contest for your brief, explain why the possibility of transferring second preferences changes how candidates in the first round should be expected to behave.

answer.exemplar: In a first round the vote is a sorting exercise, and candidates who expect to be eliminated have every reason to look for supporters who would transfer to them in the runoff. A candidate who loses on the first ballot can therefore build a constituency of second preferences, and a candidate who is kept out of the second round has an incentive to recommend somebody rather than to split the vote in a way that hands it to a rival. Strategically this rewards candidate compatibility over ideological purity: the candidate who is broadly acceptable to the voters of an eliminated rival is safer than the one who is merely second in the count. The system thereby rewards coalition-building in advance rather than only at the moment of elimination.

questions.explanation: Because eliminated candidates can direct supporters to a preferred rival, the first round also shapes the second ballot. That rewards broad acceptability and early coalition-building over pure ideological positioning.
questions.hint: Ask what eliminated candidates do with their votes.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the barrier produced by a tacit agreement between two incumbents.
questions.stem: A regional party system has just two parties, both of which are in the legislature, and they agree never to contest each other's strongholds. What kind of barrier to entry does this arrangement create?

options.text: A legal barrier, because the two parties have signed a binding agreement in writing.
options.misconception: assumes a tacit agreement must be written and binding

options.text: A social and reputational barrier, because entering a stronghold invites exclusion.
A scale barrier, because two parties already divide all the available resources.
options.misconception: treats a division of seats as a cost advantage

options.text: A legal barrier, because the standing orders forbid any other party from standing.
options.misconception: invents a standing order that the scenario never mentions

questions.explanation: A tacit agreement to avoid each other's strongholds raises the personal cost of contesting them. No legal rule changes, so new entrants are deterred by the expectation of exclusion.
questions.hint: Notice that no rule was actually changed.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Infer the voting system from the pattern of seat winners.
questions.stem: A party wins every district in which it is the second preference of more voters than any other party, and wins none where it is first. What does this pattern indicate about the electoral system in use?

options.text: The system awards seats on first preferences, and the party is failing to win any.
options.misconception: ignores the possibility that second preferences decide seats

options.text: The system uses proportional representation, and the party is over-represented.
options.misconception: assumes seat patterns prove a proportional outcome

options.text: The system decides seats on later preferences, which suits a party strong in transfers.
The party has a discipline problem, since it is not converting its support at the first count.
options.misconception: blames party organisation for an electoral rule

questions.explanation: Winning only where the party is second indicates that later preferences decide the seats. That suits parties whose voters are acceptable second choices to other voters.
questions.hint: Look at which preference decides the seat.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Assess whether a party has built a durable organisation rather than a mobilisation.

stimulus.body: Membership review: 'Of 2,800 paid members, 2,150 have not taken part in a branch meeting for over two years, and 1,940 joined in the two years after the river dredging campaign ended. Only 61 members attended the policy session that drafted the current programme, and 44 of those were present at the founding meeting. The review notes that a separate organisation with similar single-campaign origins now has a permanent secretariat and an annual conference.'

questions.stem: What does the membership review suggest about the party's organisational development?

options.text: The party is growing rapidly, since most members joined after the dredging campaign ended.
options.misconception: treats post-campaign recruitment as organisational development

options.text: The party has too many members, because 2,150 never attend branch meetings.
options.misconception: assumes inactive members weaken the organisation

options.text: The policy session was too large, because sixty-one members is an unwieldy number.
options.misconception: judges a policy session by its attendance size alone

options.text: The party lacks a durable organisation, unlike the comparable body with a permanent secretariat.

questions.explanation: A membership dominated by post-campaign recruits, with no branch activity, is a mobilisation not an organisation. The comparable body's permanent secretariat shows what durable structure actually requires.
questions.hint: Compare the two bodies' structures.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Design a two-chamber arrangement that improves scrutiny without creating delay.
questions.stem: Your design brief asks for a two-chamber arrangement that improves the quality of scrutiny without introducing unacceptable delay. Propose how you would divide the work between the chambers, and defend the arrangement against the usual objections.

answer.exemplar: Divide the work by function rather than by size, and let the smaller chamber do what the full chamber does badly. Detail, technical amendment and evidence gathering suit a body that sits longer, in smaller groups, without the incentive to make headlines. The larger chamber should then do what it does well: set the principle, hear the argument in public, and take the final decision. Two safeguards keep the arrangement from becoming a machine for delay. First, set a hard deadline after which a measure must move or lapse, so a minor chamber cannot hold the programme hostage. Second, allow the larger chamber to overrule the smaller by a supermajority, which preserves a check while making obstruction visible and costly. The familiar objection is that a second stage slows legislation, but delay comes from open-ended amendment rights, not from having two stages at all.

questions.explanation: A functional split matches each chamber to what it does best, while deadlines and a costly override prevent vetoes. Delay comes from open-ended amendment rights rather than from the existence of two stages.
questions.hint: Divide by function, then close the loopholes.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why formal openness does not guarantee an open market.
questions.stem: A competition authority finds that a new firm can register as a party, contest every district, and appear on the ballot, yet gains no contestant in any election. What best explains this outcome?

options.text: The costs of competing are high enough that entry is not worthwhile, despite formal openness.
The legal rules must still be blocking registration, because no candidate appeared.
options.misconception: treats a poor showing as proof of a legal bar

options.text: The party system is competitive, since the barrier has been removed entirely.
options.misconception: assumes formal openness means the absence of barriers

options.text: Voters rejected every candidate, so the obstacle lies with the electorate alone.
options.misconception: ignores the cost side of the entry decision

questions.explanation: Formal openness removes the legal barrier but leaves the economic one, and entry needs a plausible return. Without a realistic chance of seats the cost of contesting is not justified, so the market stays closed.
questions.hint: Ask whether a legal rule is still in the way.
